newsitem.title: USA: Senate to begin probe into Clinton fund-raising.
newsitem.headline: Senate to begin probe into Clinton fund-raising.

text.p: The U.S. Senate opens nearly four weeks of potentially explosive hearings on Tuesday on President Bill Clinton's campaign ties to foreign money, with current and former senior White House aides ordered to appear before investigators.

Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson, who served as Republican counsel for the 1973 Senate Watergate hearings, will gavel open the long-awaited oversight hearings five months after they were initially expected to get under way -- and observers are expecting mudslinging on both sides.

The hearings by the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee will seek, among other things, to determine whether China or other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by making large donations to Democrats in the 1996 campaign.

Among key witnesses subpoenaed to appear are four aides close to Clinton and the Democratic party: Harold Ickes, formerly Clinton's deputy chief of staff, Don Fowler, former Democratic National Committee co-chairman, long-time Clinton confidant Bruce Lindsey and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton's former chief of staff Maggie Williams. The first witnesses will appear on Wednesday.
But three other key witnesses central to the probe are either in Asia or have pledged not to testify without immunity.
The president is conveniently out of town.

Clinton, whose popularity has remained buoyant despite the seemingly endless stream of revelations on the fund-raising controversy, is in Madrid trying to convince Washington's partners to limit expansion of NATO to three former Soviet bloc countries: Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

The president has tried to cast NATO expansion as an historic accomplishment akin to the Marshall Plan adopted after the Second World War, but back at home, Thompson and his colleagues will be asking tough questions about Democratic fund-raising tactics such as sleepovers for big donors in the White House's Lincoln Bedroom.

The White House has dismissed the Senate investigation as "all politics" and plans an aggressive counter-assault against allegations of illegal and improper campaign fundraising practices in the 1996 presidential election.

In fact, CBS-TV's "Evening News" reported on Monday that U.S. businessman Michael Kojima, who made a $500,000 donation to the Republican Party in 1992, funneled in the money from Japanese businessmen who sought to profit from Republican connections.
The report said Kojima flew in a group of Japanese businessmen for the 1992 Republican fund-raiser after asking them for hundreds of thousands of dollars for the chance to meet President George Bush.

Meanwhile, the Washington Post, in its Tuesday editions, detailed the campaign contributions received by the nine Republican and seven Democratic senators on the committee, noting that "every senator on the panel has firsthand experience with the pressures and temptations of the campaign money chase."

Thompson, a smooth-talking former actor rumored to have presidential ambitions of his own, has vowed a fair inquiry but made clear Democrats would get the brunt of the attention because most of the allegations so far have been made against them.
"I'm not going to try to generate a lot of time and effort just trying to find something in the name of so-called balance," he told CNN.
